readerTitle: Everyone picks the cheapest package. Now what?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사무실 단체 점심 케이터링, B2B 서비스 + 식음료) · 모든 수치와 결과는 설명용
insight: 메뉴가 안 팔릴 때 가격을 내리기 전에, 고객이 먼저 보는 숫자와 비교 대상, '무료'가 붙는 자리를 바꿔 본다.
misconception: 원하는 상품이 안 팔리면 그 상품의 가격을 내리거나 싼 상품을 없애야 한다.

sources.text: Tversky, A. & Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases. Science. (앵커링 개념 배경)
Huber, J., Payne, J. W. & Puto, C. (1982). Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives. Journal of Consumer Research. (디코이 효과 개념 배경)
Shampanier, K., Mazar, N. & Ariely, D. (2007). Zero as a Special Price. Marketing Science. (무료의 힘 개념 배경)
모든 수치와 결과는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 가격 차이 확인: Basic $14 → Classic $19 = $5 차이. 디코이 'Basic + dessert' $18 → Classic $19 = $1 차이. 차트 합계 변경 전 70+20+10=100%, 변경 후 35+5+50+10=100%.
'무료가 같은 금액의 할인보다 강하게 끈다'는 문장은 Shampanier, Mazar & Ariely(2007)의 일반적 결론을 단순화한 표현입니다. 구체적 효과 크기는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 논문 요지를 다시 확인하세요.
세 가지 개입의 결과(주문 비중 변화)는 실제 연구 결과가 아니라 시뮬레이션용 가상 결과입니다. 카드에 'Say you…'와 illustrative 라벨로 표시했습니다.

cards.title: Everyone picks the cheapest package. Now what?
body: Lena runs a catering business that delivers lunch to offices. Her menu has three packages: **Basic** at $14 a person, **Classic** at $19 and **Premium** at $25.
Classic is the lunch she's proudest of, and it leaves her a healthy margin. Yet about 7 in 10 orders are Basic. Your job: help her fix the menu without cutting a single price.

image.label: Office lunch spread with three package cards, one stacked much higher
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실 회의 테이블 위 케이터링 도시락. 옆에 세 장의 패키지 카드 'Basic $14', 'Classic $19', 'Premium $25'. 'Basic' 카드 앞에만 주문서가 높이 쌓여 있음. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: The menu starts at $14.
body: Her PDF menu and website list the packages cheapest first: Basic, Classic, Premium. Office managers read from the top and often stop at the first option that fits the budget.

options.text: Lower Classic to $17 to close the gap with Basic
options.feedback: Some clients would switch up. But you give away $2 on every Classic order, including from clients who happily paid $19.

options.text: List the packages from most to least expensive
options.feedback: Buyers now see $25 first, so $19 feels moderate and $14 feels thin. Same prices, a different first number.

options.text: Drop Basic so every order starts at $19
options.feedback: Some clients will upgrade. Others with a fixed budget will call a cheaper caterer, and you lose them entirely.

cards.title: Classic still looks like a stretch.
body: Say you chose to reorder. Classic orders tick up, but Basic still leads.
Basic is sandwiches and salad. Classic adds hot mains and dessert. Many buyers can't tell if that $5 jump is worth it. What do you add?

image.label: Menu with four packages, a new option sitting just below Classic
image.brief: 메뉴판 인포그래픽. 위에서부터 'Premium $25', 'Classic $19', 'Basic + dessert $18', 'Basic $14'. 'Basic + dessert'는 흐리게, 'Classic'은 강조 테두리. Classic과 $18 옵션 사이에 '+$1: hot mains' 작은 화살표.

options.feedback: Few will pick it. Its job is to make Classic, with hot mains *and* dessert for $1 more, look like the obvious upgrade.

options.text: More sides in Basic, so it feels generous
options.feedback: Clients will like it, but you've made the cheapest package even more tempting and squeezed your thinnest margin.
Labels do guide the eye. But Basic is the most popular, so the badge isn't true. A "Chef's pick" label would be honest.

cards.title: The $30 line at the bottom.
body: Say you chose to add the $18 option. Classic is gaining.
But every quote ends with a $30 delivery fee, and office managers often push back on that line, not on the food. What do you change?

image.label: A quote with the delivery fee line crossed out and marked free
image.brief: 견적서 클로즈업. 'Classic × 30 people $570' 아래 'Delivery $30' 줄에 줄이 그어지고 'FREE' 스탬프. 옆의 'Basic' 견적서에는 배달비가 그대로 남아 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

options.text: Cut the fee to $15 on all orders
options.feedback: Cheaper, but it's still a fee buyers notice and question. You lose $15 an order and steer no one.

options.text: Free delivery on Classic and Premium; Basic keeps the fee
options.feedback: *Free* gets far more attention than a small discount, and now it sits on the package you want to sell. You give up $30 only on orders that earn you more.
Buyers will love it, but you lose $30 on every Basic order, your thinnest margin, and nothing nudges anyone up.

cards.title: Same prices, a different mix.
body: Say you made all three moves. Two months later, here's how orders split.
Food revenue per person rises from about **$16.10 to $17.80**, and no price went up.
cards.softwareNote: A pricing page works the same way. Show the top plan first, add an option that makes your target plan a clear step up, and put the free extra, like setup help, on the plan you want customers to choose.

cards.title: You changed three things at once.
body: Lena can't tell which move did the work. To find out, she'd change one thing at a time and compare a few weeks before and after.

These nudges also move only buyers who were close to deciding. They can't save a lunch clients don't enjoy. And the decoy must be a real option you'll happily serve. Office managers order every week, and they notice games.

cards.title: Change what buyers see before you change the price.
body: Each decision used one idea from this unit:
list: **Most expensive first:** *anchoring*. The first price sets the reference.
**Basic + dessert at $18:** the *decoy effect*. A nearly-as-good option makes the target look like a bargain.
**Free delivery on Classic:** the *power of free*. Zero pulls harder than a small discount, so put it where you want buyers to go.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** open your own menu or price list. Which price does a customer see first, and is it the one you want them to compare against?
